questions.question: A light horizontal beam is pivoted at its centre. A 40 N downward force acts 0.75 m to the left of the pivot. A 25 N downward force acts 0.60 m to the right. What additional downward force must act 0.30 m to the right to establish rotational equilibrium?

M_C=25(0.60)=15 N m


Let the additional force be F. Its clockwise moment is 0.30F.

For equilibrium,


30=15+0.30F



0.30F=15



F=50 N

questions.title: — The Inclined Ladder Against a Smooth Wall
questions.question: A uniform ladder rests against a smooth vertical wall and a rough horizontal floor. Its weight is 200 N, acting at its midpoint. The horizontal reaction at the wall is 60 N. The ladder makes an angle of 45^° with the floor. Find the vertical reaction of the floor, assuming the ladder is in equilibrium.
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="25" y1="165" x2="295" y2="165" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="245" y1="25" x2="245" y2="165" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3" /><line x1="80" y1="165" x2="245" y2="25" stroke="#b77935" stroke-width="7" stroke-linecap="round" /><circle cx="80" cy="165" r="4" fill="currentColor" /><line x1="245" y1="25" x2="282" y2="25" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2.5" /><polygon points="290,25 278,19 278,31" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="253" y="15" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Reaction R</text><line x1="165" y1="95" x2="165" y2="130" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2.5" /><polygon points="165,138 159,126 171,126" fill="#d97706" /><text x="174" y="119" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">W = 200 N</text><text x="37" y="185" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Floor</text><text x="258" y="110" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Smooth wall</text></svg>
questions.explanation:
The wall is smooth, so its reaction is horizontal. It has no vertical component. Therefore, the floor must balance the entire weight vertically:


R_V-W=0



R_V=200 N


The horizontal reaction determines the frictional force at the floor, not the vertical reaction.

**Concept tested:** Resolving forces in equilibrium when the wall is smooth.

questions.title: — A Force Applied at Different Angles
questions.question: A rigid rod of length 0.8 m is pivoted at O. A force of 50 N acts at its free end at 60^° to the rod. The force is then changed to 30 N at 90^°. By how much does the moment change?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="20" y1="110" x2="300" y2="110" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3" /><circle cx="35" cy="110" r="5" fill="currentColor" /><text x="20" y="130" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">O</text><line x1="35" y1="110" x2="275" y2="110" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="275" y1="110" x2="225" y2="24" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="221,17 222,30 233,24" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="235" y="22" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">F = 50 N</text><path d="M245 110 A30 30 0 0 0 260 84" fill="none" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><text x="250" y="101" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">60°</text><text x="105" y="100" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">0.8 m</text></svg>

options.text: It increases by 4.8 N m.
It decreases by 4.8 N m.
It increases by 16 N m.
It remains unchanged.

questions.explanation:
Initially,


M₁=50(0.8)sin60^°
=20sqrt3≈34.64 N m


Finally,


M₂=30(0.8)sin90^°=24 N m


Therefore, the moment actually **decreases by 10.64 N m**. None of the options is correct.

**Concept tested:** Comparing moments when both force magnitude and angle change.

questions.title: — The Balanced Signboard
questions.question: A light signboard is balanced about a pivot. A 60 N load acts 0.5 m to the left of the pivot, while an unknown load W acts 1.5 m to the right. Find W.
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="25" y1="28" x2="295" y2="28" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3" /><rect x="45" y="28" width="230" height="12" fill="#999" /><line x1="80" y1="40" x2="80" y2="84" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="80,91 74,79 86,79" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="55" y="108" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">60 N</text><line x1="230" y1="40" x2="230" y2="84" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="230,91 224,79 236,79" fill="#d97706" /><text x="213" y="108" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">W</text><text x="57" y="20" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">0.5 m</text><text x="210" y="20" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">1.5 m</text><path d="M145 40 L160 75 L175 40 Z" fill="#777" stroke="currentColor" /><text x="141" y="91" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Pivot</text></svg>
questions.explanation:
For equilibrium, clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment.


60(0.5)=W(1.5)



W=(30 / 1.5)=20 N


**Concept tested:** Finding an unknown load when the load arms differ greatly.

questions.title: — The Couple on a Steering Wheel
questions.question: Two equal, opposite parallel forces of 15 N act on a steering wheel. The perpendicular separation of their lines of action is 0.4 m. If both forces are doubled and their separation is halved, what is the new moment of the couple?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="155" cy="75" r="55" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="4" /><circle cx="155" cy="75" r="6" fill="currentColor" /><line x1="100" y1="75" x2="210" y2="75" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="100" y1="75" x2="100" y2="25" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="100,18 94,30 106,30" fill="#2878c8" /><line x1="210" y1="75" x2="210" y2="125" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="210,132 204,120 216,120" fill="#d97706" /><text x="63" y="20" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">15 N</text><text x="215" y="134" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">15 N</text><text x="118" y="146" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Separation = 0.4 m</text></svg>

options.text: 3 N m
6 N m
12 N m
24 N m

questions.explanation:
Original couple moment:


M=15(0.4)=6 N m


New force =30 N, and new separation =0.2 m.


M'=30(0.2)=6 N m


Doubling the force while halving the separation leaves the moment unchanged.

**Concept tested:** How two simultaneous changes affect the moment of a couple.

questions.title: — The Rod Suspended by Two Strings
questions.question: A uniform horizontal rod weighing 120 N is suspended by two vertical strings attached symmetrically at its ends. A further 40 N weight is attached exactly at its centre. Find the tension in each string.
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="20" y1="20" x2="300" y2="20" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="65" y1="20" x2="65" y2="75" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="255" y1="20" x2="255" y2="75" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="35" y1="75" x2="285" y2="75" stroke="#b77935" stroke-width="7" /><line x1="160" y1="75" x2="160" y2="116" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="160,123 154,111 166,111" fill="#d97706" /><text x="173" y="110" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">120 N</text><text x="42" y="12" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">T₁</text><text x="263" y="12" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">T₂</text></svg>

options.text: 40 N and 120 N
60 N and 100 N
80 N and 80 N
120 N and 120 N

questions.explanation:
Total downward force:


120+40=160 N


By symmetry, the two tensions are equal:


T₁=T₂=(160 / 2)
=80 N


**Concept tested:** Combining symmetry, force balance and the weight of a uniform rod.

questions.title: — The Child on a Seesaw Moves
questions.question: A 30 kg child sits 2 m from the fulcrum on one side of a seesaw. A 20 kg child sits 3 m from the fulcrum on the opposite side. The seesaw is initially horizontal. The 30 kg child moves 0.5 m farther away. What happens to the net moment? Take g=10 m s^.
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 140" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="20" y1="45" x2="300" y2="45" stroke="#b77935" stroke-width="6" /><path d="M145 92 L160 49 L175 92 Z" fill="#999" stroke="currentColor" /><circle cx="60" cy="36" r="9" fill="#2878c8" /><circle cx="245" cy="36" r="9" fill="#d97706" /><text x="35" y="20" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">30 kg</text><text x="220" y="20" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">20 kg</text><text x="28" y="73" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">2 m</text><text x="230" y="73" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">3 m</text><text x="140" y="108" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Fulcrum</text></svg>

options.text: It becomes 150 N m towards the 30 kg child.
It becomes 150 N m towards the 20 kg child.
It remains zero.
It becomes 300 N m towards the 30 kg child.

questions.explanation:
Initially, the moments balance:


300(2)=200(3)=600 N m


After moving, the first child is 2.5 m away:


M₁=300(2.5)=750 N m


The opposing moment remains 600 N m.


M_{net}=750-600=150 N m


**Concept tested:** The effect of changing only one person's distance from a pivot.

questions.title: — The Crane Boom
questions.question: A crane boom pivots at a fixed point. A 400 N load acts vertically downward at a horizontal distance of 3 m from the pivot. The boom itself is light. Calculate the moment of the load about the pivot.

options.text: 400 N m
800 N m

questions.explanation:
Because the load acts vertically, the perpendicular distance is the horizontal reach of 3 m.


M=400(3)=1,200 N m


**Concept tested:** Identifying the correct perpendicular distance for a vertical force acting on an inclined boom.

questions.title: — The Door with Two Handles
questions.question: Two people push a door at different heights. Each applies a 10 N force perpendicular to the door, in the same direction, and each force has a perpendicular distance of 0.5 m from the hinge axis. What is the total moment about the hinge?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="50" y="20" width="220" height="110" fill="#d6b77b" stroke="#806b44" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="50" y1="20" x2="50" y2="130" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="5" /><circle cx="220" cy="50" r="5" fill="#d97706" /><circle cx="220" cy="100" r="5" fill="#d97706" /><line x1="220" y1="50" x2="265" y2="50" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="273,50 261,44 261,56" fill="#2878c8" /><line x1="220" y1="100" x2="265" y2="100" stroke="#16856b" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="273,100 261,94 261,106" fill="#16856b" /><text x="235" y="40" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">10 N</text><text x="235" y="90" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">10 N</text><text x="85" y="145" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Two handles at different heights</text></svg>

options.text: 0 N m
2.5 N m
5 N m
10 N m

questions.explanation:
Each force produces


M=10(0.5)=5 N m


Since both moments act in the same rotational direction, they add:


M_{total}=5+5=10 N m


**Concept tested:** Adding moments that act in the same direction.

Taking moments about the pivot:


5(40-10)=2(50-40)+3(x-40)



150=20+3(x-40)

options.text: 35 N downward
45 N downward
55 N downward

questions.explanation: By the principle of moments: Total Clockwise Moment = Total Anticlockwise Moment. Distance of 40 N weight from pivot (40 cm) = 40 cm - 0 cm = 40 cm. Anticlockwise moment = 40 N × 40 cm = 1,600 N cm. The weight of the rod (80 N) acts through its centre of gravity G at distance x from end A, so its distance from the pivot is (x - 40) cm. Clockwise moment = 80 N × (x - 40) cm. Equating moments: 80 × (x - 40) = 1,600 => x - 40 = 20 => x = 60 cm from end A.

questions.title: Metre Rule with Its Own Weight
questions.question: A uniform metre rule of mass 100 g is balanced horizontally on a knife-edge placed at the 45 cm mark when a mass m is suspended from the 20 cm mark. Calculate the value of the mass m.

questions.explanation: Because the metre rule is uniform, its mass of 100 g acts through its centre of gravity at the 50 cm mark. Distance of centre of gravity from pivot = 50 cm - 45 cm = 5 cm (clockwise arm). Clockwise moment = 100 g × 5 cm = 500 g cm. Distance of suspended mass m from pivot = 45 cm - 20 cm = 25 cm (anticlockwise arm). Anticlockwise moment = m × 25 cm. By the principle of moments: m × 25 = 500 => m = 500 / 25 = 20 g.

questions.title: Why was the classification of elements necessary?
questions.question: Why was the classification of elements necessary?

options.text: To prove that all elements have identical chemical properties
To arrange elements according to their physical states alone
To organize elements systematically and reveal relationships among their properties
To eliminate the need to study individual elements

questions.explanation:
As the number of known elements increased, scientists needed a systematic method to organize them and identify similarities, differences, and periodic patterns.

**Tempting distractor:** Option B is too restrictive. Classification considers atomic properties and chemical behaviour, not merely physical state.

questions.title: Which statement correctly describes Dobereiner's triads?
questions.question: Which statement correctly describes Dobereiner's triads?

options.text: Elements were arranged in groups of three with related properties, and the middle atomic mass was approximately the mean of the other two
Every third element had exactly the same atomic mass as the first
Elements were arranged in increasing atomic number in groups of eight
All elements in a triad had identical valencies and atomic masses

questions.explanation:
Dobereiner grouped certain chemically similar elements into triads. The atomic mass of the middle element was approximately the arithmetic mean of the other two.

**Tempting distractor:** Option C describes a feature associated with Newlands' Law of Octaves, not Dobereiner's triads.

questions.title: Why did Newlands' Law of Octaves fail for heavier elements?
questions.question: Why did Newlands' Law of Octaves fail for heavier elements?

options.text: It arranged elements according to atomic number
It applied only to noble gases
It required all elements to have the same atomic mass
The resemblance of every eighth element did not hold consistently beyond the lighter elements

questions.explanation:
Newlands observed recurring properties when elements were arranged in increasing atomic mass, particularly among lighter elements. The pattern did not work consistently for heavier elements, and his arrangement left no suitable gaps for undiscovered elements.

**Tempting distractor:** Option A is incorrect because Newlands used atomic mass, not atomic number.

questions.title: Which was a major strength of Mendeleev's periodic table?
questions.question: Which was a major strength of Mendeleev's periodic table?

options.text: It placed every element in its modern atomic-number position
It left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties
It explained the electronic configurations of all elements
It eliminated every anomaly involving isotopes

questions.explanation:
Mendeleev deliberately left gaps where he believed undiscovered elements belonged. His predictions for elements later identified as scandium, gallium, and germanium were important successes.

**Tempting distractor:** Option A describes the principle of the modern periodic table, which is based on atomic number.

questions.title: What was the central contribution of Henry Moseley to periodic classification?
questions.question: What was the central contribution of Henry Moseley to periodic classification?

options.text: He established the Law of Octaves
He grouped elements into triads
He demonstrated the importance of atomic number in determining the correct order of elements
He discovered the noble gases as a group

questions.explanation:
Moseley's work on characteristic X-ray spectra established atomic number as the fundamental basis for ordering elements. This helped resolve anomalies in Mendeleev's atomic-mass arrangement.

**Tempting distractor:** Option B refers to Dobereiner, not Moseley.

questions.title: Board-style Predicting the position of an element
questions.question: An element X has the electronic configuration 2,8,2. Which set of statements is correct? 1. X belongs to Period 3. 2. X belongs to Group 2. 3. X is expected to form X^. 4. Its oxide has the formula XO₂.

options.text: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only

questions.explanation:
Three occupied shells place X in Period 3. Two valence electrons place it in Group 2, and it commonly loses both to form X²⁺. Oxygen forms O²⁻, so the oxide formula is XO, not XO₂.

**Tempting distractor:** Option D overlooks charge balance in the oxide formula.

questions.title: Board-style Identifying an incorrect periodic trend
questions.question: Which arrangement is incorrect?

options.text: Atomic size: Na > Mg > Al
Metallic character: Na > Mg > Al
First ionisation energy: Na < Mg < Al
Number of occupied shells: Na = Mg = Al

questions.explanation:
Although first ionisation energy generally increases across a period, aluminium's first ionisation energy is slightly lower than magnesium's because aluminium's first removed electron is in a higher-energy 3p subshell.

The correct order is Na < Al < Mg.

**Tempting distractor:** Option C looks consistent with the broad left-to-right trend but misses the magnesium–aluminium exception.

questions.title: Board-style Comparing elements in the same group
questions.question: Lithium, sodium and potassium belong to Group 1. Which sequence correctly describes their general trend down the group?

options.text: Atomic size decreases; electron loss becomes more difficult
Atomic size increases; metallic character decreases
Atomic size increases; the outer electron is generally lost more easily
Atomic size remains constant; ionisation energy increases

questions.explanation:
Each successive element has an additional occupied shell. Greater shielding and increased distance of the valence electron from the nucleus generally make electron loss easier, so metallic reactivity increases down Group 1.

**Tempting distractor:** Option B correctly states the size trend but reverses the trend in metallic character.

questions.title: Board-style Comparing halogens
questions.question: Fluorine, chlorine and bromine are placed in the same group. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Fluorine has the largest atomic radius
Bromine attracts an incoming electron more strongly than fluorine in the usual group trend
All three elements have seven valence electrons
Their metallic character increases upward in the group

questions.explanation:
Group 17 elements have seven valence electrons. Down the group, atomic size increases and the tendency to attract an incoming electron generally weakens; halogens are nonmetals.

**Tempting distractor:** Option B reverses the usual trend in electron-attracting ability down the halogen group.

questions.title: Board-style Evaluating an ionisation-energy explanation
questions.question: A student claims: “The first ionisation energy of every successive element across a period must be greater than that of the element immediately before it.” Which response is best?

options.text: Correct, because atomic number increases
Incorrect, because subshell energies and electron-pair repulsion can produce exceptions
Correct, because atomic radius always decreases without exception
Incorrect, because ionisation energy decreases uniformly across every period

questions.explanation:
First ionisation energy generally rises across a period, but the trend is not perfectly uniform. The Be–B and N–O comparisons illustrate important exceptions due to subshell energy and electron pairing.

**Tempting distractor:** Option A confuses a general relationship with a strict rule.

questions.title: Determining the atomic number from an ion
questions.question: An element X forms X^, which contains 18 electrons. Its neutral atom has three occupied shells. What are the atomic number and group of X?

options.text: Atomic number 16, Group 16
Atomic number 20, Group 2
Atomic number 18, Group 18
Atomic number 16, Group 2

questions.explanation:
1. X²⁻ has gained two electrons, so the neutral atom contains 18-2=16 electrons.
2. Therefore, its atomic number is 16, identifying sulphur.
3. Sulphur has configuration 2,8,6, placing it in Group 16.

Option B incorrectly treats the ion's electron count as its atomic number.

options.text: Period 3, Group 17

- Valence electrons =7, so Group 10+7=17.
- The configuration identifies bromine, atomic number 35.

questions.title: Calculating the number of electrons in a cation
questions.question: A neutral atom has atomic number 20. It loses two electrons to form a stable ion. How many electrons remain, and which noble gas has the same electronic configuration?

options.text: 20 electrons; argon
18 electrons; neon
18 electrons; argon
22 electrons; calcium

questions.explanation:
1. A neutral atom with atomic number 20 contains 20 electrons.
2. Losing two electrons gives 20-2=18 electrons.
3. The resulting configuration is 2,8,8, the same as argon.

Option A ignores the electron loss. The number of protons remains 20.

questions.title: Determining the formula of a compound
questions.question: Element P has atomic number 12, and element Q has atomic number 17. Assuming they form a compound by electron transfer, what is its simplest formula?

options.text: PQ
P_2Q
PQ₃
PQ₂

questions.explanation:
- P, magnesium, has configuration 2,8,2 and forms P²⁺.
- Q, chlorine, has configuration 2,8,7 and forms Q⁻.
- Two Q⁻ ions balance one P²⁺ ion.

Thus, the formula is PQ₂, or MgCl₂. Option A fails to balance the ionic charges.

=(88 / 2)=44

options.text: It was based on atomic number and failed because atomic numbers were unknown.
It worked reasonably well for lighter elements but did not satisfactorily accommodate the heavier elements.
It left deliberate gaps for undiscovered elements and accurately predicted their properties.
It placed all known elements in 18 groups and seven periods.

questions.explanation: Newlands arranged elements by increasing atomic mass and proposed that every eighth element had similar properties. options.text: It has no electron in its outermost shell.
It is a non-metal with one electron and can lose or gain an electron in different chemical situations, so its properties do not fully match those of Group 1.

It has a complete outer shell identical to neon.

Hydrogen has the configuration 1, with only one electron. Although it is often placed above Group 1, it is a non-metal and can form both H⁺ and H⁻ in appropriate compounds. Option A is wrong because its only shell contains one electron.

options.text: S is more acidic than P because its pH is closer to 7.
Q contains no hydrogen ions because it is neutral.
R is alkaline, while P is more acidic than S.
P and R are both acidic because neither has pH 7.

questions.explanation:
At room temperature, pH below 7 indicates an acidic solution, pH 7 indicates neutrality, and pH above 7 indicates an alkaline solution. Therefore, P (pH 2) is more acidic than S (pH 5), while R (pH 11) is alkaline. Neutral water still contains hydrogen ions, represented in aqueous solution as hydronium ions, H_3O⁺, and hydroxide ions, OH⁻, in equal concentrations. Neutral does not mean ion-free.

options.text: Tube B is neutral, Tube A is acidic, and Tube C is alkaline.
Tube A must contain a strong acid, while Tube D must contain a weak acid.
Tube C must contain sodium hydroxide, NaOH, and Tube B must contain pure water, H_2O.
Tube D is more alkaline than Tube C because yellow occurs before blue in the colour chart.

questions.explanation:
Universal indicator generally shows red in strongly acidic solutions, yellow in acidic solutions, green near pH 7, and blue in alkaline solutions. The colours indicate approximate pH, not the chemical identity or concentration of a solution. Thus, red alone cannot prove that an acid is strong, and green does not prove that a sample is pure water.

questions.diagramSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 460 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc; border-radius:8px; border:1px solid #cbd5e1; font-family:system-ui, sans-serif;">
      <text x="230" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#0f172a">Collection of HCl Gas: Upward Displacement of Air</text>
      <!-- Delivery tube entering jar -->
      <path d="M 80 50 L 170 50 L 170 145" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="3"/>
      <!-- Upright Gas Jar -->
      <g transform="translate(150, 45)">
        <rect x="0" y="0" width="45" height="110" rx="3" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/>
        <!-- Heavy HCl filling bottom -->
        <rect x="2" y="55" width="41" height="53" fill="#fef08a" opacity="0.5"/>
        <text x="22" y="85" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="800" fill="#854d0e">HCl Gas</text>
      </g>
      <!-- Displaced Air Arrow -->
      <defs>
        <marker id="arrAir" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="5" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto-start-reverse">
          <path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="#3b82f6"/>
        </marker>
      </defs>
      <path d="M 185 60 Q 210 35 230 45" fill="none" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.5" marker-end="url(#arrAir)"/>
      <text x="250" y="45" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#2563eb">Air displaced upwards ↑</text>
      <!-- Explanatory Box -->
      <rect x="230" y="70" width="200" height="85" rx="5" fill="#eff6ff" stroke="#bfdbfe"/>
      <text x="330" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#1e40af">Why This Method?</text>
      <text x="240" y="112" font-size="9.5" fill="#334155">• HCl Vapour Density = 18.25</text>
      <text x="240" y="127" font-size="9.5" fill="#334155">• Air Vapour Density = 14.4</text>
      <text x="240" y="142" font-size="9.5" font-weight="600" fill="#dc2626">• Cannot collect over water (Highly soluble!)</text>
      <text x="230" y="180" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#475569">HCl is 1.28 times denser than air and settles at the bottom of an upright jar</text>
    </svg>

options.text: Downward delivery because HCl is lighter than air and practically insoluble in water.
Collection over water because HCl does not support combustion.
Upward delivery because HCl is lighter than air, although it dissolves readily in water.
Upward delivery, or downward displacement of air, because HCl is heavier than air; it cannot conveniently be collected over water because it is extremely soluble in water.

questions.explanation:
The vapour density of HCl is 18.25, and the gas is heavier than air. Therefore, it is collected by downward displacement of air, also called upward delivery. Its solubility—about 450 volumes of HCl per volume of water—rules out collection over water. Option C identifies the method but reverses the density relationship.

options.text: Concentration by removing gangue for a second time.
Refining the impure metal before it has been produced.
Conversion of the concentrated ore into its oxide.
Reduction of the ore to metal followed by oxidation.

questions.explanation:
The usual sequence is concentration → conversion to oxide → reduction to metal → refining. The conversion stage prepares the concentrated ore for reduction. Option B incorrectly places refining before the metal has been obtained.

questions.title: Froth-Flotation Process
questions.question: Refer to the metallurgical diagram shown. Which ore is most suitable for concentration by the process shown?
questions.diagramSvg: Sulphide Ore: Wetted by pine oil Rises with foam / froth • Gangue: Wetted by water Sinks to tank floor Applicable to Zinc Blende (ZnS), Galena (PbS), Copper Pyrites (CuFeS₂)

options.text: Zinc blende, ZnS.
Calamine, ZnCO₃.
Bauxite, Al₂O₃·2H₂O.
Native gold, Au.

questions.explanation:
Froth flotation is particularly suitable for sulphide ores. Zinc blende, ZnS, is a sulphide ore whose particles can attach preferentially to the froth. Calamine is a carbonate ore, bauxite is a hydrated oxide ore, and native gold occurs in the free state.

questions.title: Distinguishing zinc from lead using two reagents
questions.question: Two colourless solutions, A and B, are tested with NaOH and NH₄OH. Solution A forms a white precipitate that dissolves in excess of both reagents. Solution B forms a white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH, but remains insoluble in excess NH₄OH. Which identification is correct?

      <text x="342" y="88" font-size="8.5" fill="#334155">Zn²⁺ + 2OH⁻ →</text>
      <text x="350" y="100" font-size="8.5" font-weight="700" fill="#dc2626">Zn(OH)₂↓ (White)</text>
      <text x="342" y="118" font-size="8.5" fill="#334155">Zn(OH)₂ + 2OH⁻ →</text>
      <text x="350" y="130" font-size="8.5" font-weight="700" fill="#16a34a">[Zn(OH)₄]²⁻ (Soluble)</text>

options.text: A is Pb(NO₃)₂ and B is ZnSO₄
A is ZnSO₄ and B is Pb(NO₃)₂
A is CaCl₂ and B is ZnSO₄
A is CuSO₄ and B is Pb(NO₃)₂

questions.explanation:
Both Zn²⁺ and Pb²⁺ give white hydroxide precipitates that dissolve in excess NaOH. With excess NH₄OH, however, Zn(OH)₂ dissolves to give a colourless solution, while Pb(OH)₂ remains insoluble. Therefore, A contains Zn²⁺ and B contains Pb²⁺. Option A reverses the decisive NH₄OH results.

questions.title: Identifying the deep blue solution
questions.question: A salt solution is tested in two stages: in Stage I, adding a few drops of aqueous NH₄OH produces a pale blue precipitate; in Stage II, adding excess NH₄OH dissolves the precipitate to form a deep inky blue solution. Which statement correctly explains the final stage?

options.text: Cu(OH)₂ dissolves to form a deep blue tetraamminecopper(II) complex solution.
Cu(OH)₂ dissolves in excess NaOH to form a deep blue solution.
Zn(OH)₂ changes into a deep blue zincate solution.
Pb(OH)₂ dissolves in excess NH₄OH to form a deep blue solution.

questions.explanation:
Cu²⁺ initially forms pale blue Cu(OH)₂. Excess NH₄OH dissolves it, producing a deep blue solution containing the tetraamminecopper(II) complex. Option B wrongly assigns this characteristic deep blue result to NaOH.

Fe is a Group 16 p-block element because it has six electrons outside its nucleus.

options.text: It has no electron in its outermost shell.

questions.question: A student observes that aluminium oxide reacts with both acids and bases as shown in the diagram. Which conclusion correctly identifies the chemical nature of aluminium oxide?

options.text: It is amphoteric; its behaviour cannot be classified as exclusively basic or exclusively acidic.
It is a neutral oxide because it reacts with two different substances.
It is exclusively acidic because aluminium is a metal.
It is exclusively basic because all metal oxides react only with acids.

questions.explanation:
An amphoteric oxide reacts with both acids and bases. Aluminium oxide is a standard example. Option D is an overgeneralisation: metal oxides are not all exclusively basic.

The properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic masses alone

questions.explanation:
When elements are arranged in increasing atomic number, their physical and chemical properties recur periodically because of recurring patterns in electronic configuration.

questions.question: Why is atomic number a more reliable basis for periodic classification than atomic mass?

options.text: Atomic number changes when an atom forms an ion
Atomic mass is identical for all isotopes
Atomic number determines only the physical state of an element
Atomic number identifies nuclear charge and, in a neutral atom, the electron count that determines its electronic configuration

questions.explanation:
Atomic number equals the number of protons. In a neutral atom, it also equals the number of electrons. This determines the electronic configuration and explains the periodic recurrence of chemical properties. Atomic mass does not always give the correct order for elements with anomalous mass relationships.

**Tempting distractor:** Option B is false because isotopes of the same element have different mass numbers.

options.text: Calcium, 20
Scandium, 21
Rubidium, 37
Sodium, 11

questions.explanation:
Group 1 contains Li (3), Na (11), K (19), and Rb (37). The next Group 1 element after potassium is rubidium, atomic number 37. One must not simply add one to potassium's atomic number because calcium through krypton occupy the intervening positions.

---

questions.title: Machines Question 1
questions.question: An ideal machine and a practical machine are compared while lifting the same load through the same vertical height. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Both must require the same input work, regardless of friction.
The practical machine requires less input work because it is easier to operate.
The ideal machine requires less input work because it has no energy losses.
The ideal machine and practical machine must have identical efficiencies.

questions.explanation: The ideal machine has no energy losses, so its input work equals the useful work done in raising the load. A practical machine requires additional input work to overcome friction and other losses.

questions.title: Machines Question 2
questions.question: A claw hammer is used to pull a nail out of wood. Consider the hammer as a lever, with the point of contact with the wood acting as the fulcrum. Which statement is correct?

It is a second-class lever because the nail lies between the effort and the fulcrum.
It is a third-class lever because the effort lies between the fulcrum and the nail.
It is always a third-class lever, irrespective of how it is used.

questions.explanation: In the usual nail-pulling arrangement, the contact point with the wood acts as the fulcrum, between the applied effort and the nail being pulled. The hammer therefore functions as a first-class lever.

The effort moves downward by 20 cm, and the ideal MA is 2.

questions.title: Machines Question 11
questions.question: An ideal machine has a mechanical advantage of 0.5. Which statement must be true?

options.text: The machine is incapable of lifting any load.
The effort moves through half the distance moved by the load.
The machine has an efficiency of 50%.
The effort is twice the load, and the effort moves through half the distance moved by the load.

questions.explanation: For an ideal machine, MA=VR=0.5. Thus the effort is twice the load, while the effort displacement is half the load displacement. The machine is a force reducer but may provide a speed or distance advantage.

questions.title: Machines Question 12
questions.question: A second-class lever is used to lift a load. The load is moved closer to the fulcrum without changing the effort point. Assume the effort and load positions remain on the same side of the fulcrum. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The ideal mechanical advantage increases because the load arm decreases while the effort arm stays fixed.
The ideal mechanical advantage decreases because the load arm decreases.
The ideal mechanical advantage remains unchanged because the lever class is unchanged.
The ideal mechanical advantage becomes zero because the load is closer to the fulcrum.

questions.explanation: For an ideal lever, MA=VR=effort arm/load arm. Decreasing the load arm while retaining the effort arm increases the ratio.

questions.title: Machines Question 13
questions.question: Two levers are made from identical material and have equal lengths. Lever P has a fulcrum at its centre; Lever Q has a fulcrum closer to the load. Their own weights are negligible. Which statement is necessarily correct?

options.text: P must have the greater ideal MA because its fulcrum is central.
Q can have a greater ideal MA because its effort arm is longer relative to its load arm.
Both levers must have equal ideal MA because their lengths are equal.
The ideal MA depends only on the material and length of the lever.

questions.explanation: Mechanical advantage depends on the ratio of the effort arm to the load arm, not simply on total length or material. Moving the fulcrum towards the load can increase this ratio.

questions.title: Machines Question 14
questions.question: A pulley system is arranged so that the effort is applied downward while the load rises upward. Which statement correctly distinguishes the purpose of the fixed pulleys from that of the movable pulleys in a conventional block-and-tackle system?

options.text: Fixed pulleys always double the load, while movable pulleys only change direction.
Both types of pulleys always provide the same force advantage.
Fixed pulleys can redirect the effort, while the movable block and its supporting strands provide the main ideal force advantage.
Fixed pulleys eliminate friction, while movable pulleys eliminate the need for effort.

questions.explanation: In a conventional block-and-tackle system, fixed pulleys mainly redirect the rope and make the effort more convenient. The movable block is supported by multiple rope segments, reducing the required ideal effort.

questions.title: Machines Question 16
questions.question: A load is raised through a vertical height using an inclined plane. The same load is then raised through the same height using a longer inclined plane. Both planes are assumed ideal. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The longer plane requires less effort, but the useful output work is the same.

The longer plane requires more effort because the effort travels farther.
The longer plane performs less useful output work because it is longer.

questions.explanation: The useful work in both cases is the same gain in gravitational potential energy, mgh. A longer ideal plane reduces the required effort by increasing the distance over which it acts.

questions.title: Machines Question 21
questions.question: A lever is in equilibrium under a load and an effort. The load is doubled, and the effort is also doubled. The positions of both forces and the fulcrum remain unchanged. The lever was initially in equilibrium, and its own weight is negligible. What happens?

questions.explanation: The initial clockwise and anticlockwise moments were equal. Doubling both forces doubles both moments by the same factor, preserving equilibrium.

questions.question: A student says: “A machine with a high velocity ratio must have a high mechanical advantage.” Which response is scientifically correct?

questions.explanation:
is the most appropriate?

A) The load necessarily moves farther than the effort.
B) Some input energy is dissipated through effects such as friction, so not all input work becomes useful output work.
C) The load gains more energy than the effort supplies.
D) The system must contain a third-class lever.

**Reason:** In a real machine, friction and other losses reduce useful output work. Hence efficiency is below 100%, making MA<VR.

eta=(Useful output work / Input work)×100%

questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 145" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M38 80 H307" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" stroke-linecap="round" /><path d="M38 83 L22 111 H54 Z" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" /><path d="M78 29 V72" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M72 40 L78 28 L84 40" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="78" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#2563eb">E</text><path d="M278 29 V72" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M272 62 L278 74 L284 62" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="278" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">60 N</text><text x="38" y="125" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">F</text><path d="M38 117 H78 M78 117 H278" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 3" /><text x="58" y="139" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">5 cm</text><text x="178" y="139" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">30 cm from F</text></svg>

options.text: E=360,N, VR=frac16

questions.explanation:
Taking moments about the elbow:


E×5=60×30



E=(1800 / 5)=360,N


The ideal VR is the effort-arm to load-arm ratio:


VR=(5 / 30)=frac16


This means the correct physical pair is E=360,N and VR=frac16, which is **option B**.

Option D incorrectly uses the reciprocal of VR. A third-class lever can require an effort greater than its load while providing a distance or speed advantage.

(d_E / d_L)=(40 / 10)=4

Option A takes the reciprocal. Option D confuses the effort displacement with the ratio.

questions.question: What upward effort is needed to balance the bar?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M24 70 H316" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" stroke-linecap="round" /><path d="M96 73 L79 101 H113 Z" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M24 17 V61" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M18 50 L24 62 L30 50" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="24" y="12" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="#dc2626">200 N</text><path d="M316 114 V79" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M310 90 L316 78 L322 90" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="316" y="128" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#2563eb">E</text><path d="M170 22 V60" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M164 49 L170 61 L176 49" fill="none" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="170" y="16" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="#7c3aed">100 N</text><text x="96" y="115" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">F</text><text x="24" y="145" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">A</text><text x="316" y="145" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">B</text><text x="58" y="137" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">0.5 m</text><text x="205" y="137" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">1.5 m</text></svg>
questions.explanation:
Take moments about F. The load at A produces an anticlockwise moment:


200×0.5=100,N,m


The bar’s weight acts at its centre, 1.0,m from A, which is 0.5,m to the right of F. It produces a clockwise moment of 100×0.5=50,N,m.

The effort acts 1.5,m from F and produces an anticlockwise moment:


E(1.5)+100=50


Thus,


E=-33.3,N


The negative result means the assumed upward effort cannot balance this configuration; the effort must act downward. Therefore, the question as drawn has no valid listed answer. **This item is withdrawn and will be replaced by a physically consistent question.

questions.title: Which statement correctly distinguishes the mechanical advantage of an ideal machine from that of a real machine?
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the mechanical advantage of an ideal machine from that of a real machine?

options.text: The mechanical advantage of an ideal machine must always be less than 1.
The mechanical advantage of an ideal machine equals its velocity ratio; for a real machine, it is generally smaller than its velocity ratio.
The mechanical advantage of a real machine is always equal to its velocity ratio.
The mechanical advantage of an ideal machine is always greater than its velocity ratio.

questions.explanation: An ideal machine has 100% efficiency, so MA=VR. In a real machine, energy losses make efficiency less than 100%, so MA<VR.

questions.title: A second-class lever is commonly capable of acting as a force multiplier. Which arrangement makes this possible?
questions.question: A second-class lever is commonly capable of acting as a force multiplier. Which arrangement makes this possible?

options.text: The fulcrum lies between the effort and the load.
The effort lies between the fulcrum and the load.
The effort arm is always shorter than the load arm.
The load lies between the fulcrum and the effort.

questions.explanation: In a second-class lever, the load lies between the fulcrum and the effort. Consequently, the effort arm is longer than the load arm, allowing a mechanical advantage greater than 1 for an ideal lever.

questions.title: Which statement about a third-class lever is correct?
questions.question: Which statement about a third-class lever is correct?

options.text: It has the effort between the fulcrum and the load and generally provides a speed or distance advantage rather than a force advantage.
It always has a mechanical advantage greater than 1.
It has the load between the fulcrum and the effort.
It cannot change the direction of the applied force.

questions.explanation: In a third-class lever, the effort lies between the fulcrum and the load. The effort arm is shorter than the load arm, so its ideal mechanical advantage is less than 1, but the load can move through a greater distance.

questions.title: A uniform lever is in equilibrium under several forces. Which statement about the principle of moments is correct?
questions.question: A uniform lever is in equilibrium under several forces. Which statement about the principle of moments is correct?

options.text: The sum of all upward forces must equal the sum of all downward forces, regardless of their positions.
The total clockwise moment must always be greater than the total anticlockwise moment.
The algebraic sum of moments about any chosen point is zero for rotational equilibrium.
Only the moments of forces acting perpendicular to the lever need to be considered, even when other forces have perpendicular components.

questions.explanation: For rotational equilibrium, the algebraic sum of moments about any point is zero. Forces must be considered through their perpendicular distances from the chosen pivot.

questions.question: A single fixed pulley is used to raise a load. Why can it still be useful even when its ideal mechanical advantage is 1?

It doubles the force applied by the user.
It allows the load to rise farther than the rope is pulled.
It changes the direction of the applied effort, making it more convenient to pull downward.

questions.explanation: The perpendicular distance of the force's line of action from the fulcrum is zero. Therefore, its moment about the fulcrum is zero, although the support reaction may change.

questions.question: A person uses a lever to lift a heavy load. The fulcrum is shifted closer to the load while the effort position remains fixed. Which change occurs in the ideal mechanical advantage?

options.text: It increases because the effort arm becomes longer relative to the load arm.
It decreases because the load arm becomes shorter.
It remains unchanged because the load is the same.
It becomes zero because the fulcrum has moved.

questions.explanation: For an ideal lever, MA=VR=effort arm/load arm. Shifting the fulcrum towards the load increases the effort arm and decreases the load arm, so the ratio increases.

questions.title: Movable pulley: Finding the pulley’s own weight
questions.question: A movable pulley supports a load of 280,N. The upward effort is 170,N, and the system moves at constant speed. Assuming two supporting rope segments, what is the weight of the movable pulley?
questions.explanation:
The total supported weight equals the combined tension in the two strands:


W_{total}=2E=2(170)=340,N


Therefore,


W_p=340-280=60,N


The correct answer is **C**, not B.

questions.question: A machine takes in 600,W of power and operates at 85% efficiency. What is the power dissipated through friction, sound and heating?
questions.explanation:
Useful output power:


P_{out}=0.85(600)=510,W


Wasted power:


P_{wasted}=600-510=90,W


The correct answer is **C**, not B.

questions.title: Combined numerical problem: MA, VR and efficiency
questions.question: A machine raises a load of 720,N using an effort of 180,N. During the operation, the effort moves 2.4,m while the load moves 0.6,m. Calculate its efficiency and the energy wasted if the effort completes this displacement once.
questions.explanation:
Mechanical advantage:


MA=(720 / 180)=4


Velocity ratio:


VR=(2.4 / 0.6)=4


Therefore,


eta=frac44×100=100%


Input work:


W_{in}=180(2.4)=432,J


Useful output work:


W_{out}=720(0.6)=432,J


Thus, the energy wasted is 0,J. The correct answer is **D**, not B.

questions.title: Compound machine: Two stages of mechanical advantage
questions.question: A compound machine consists of two ideal stages. The first stage has a mechanical advantage of 3, and its output drives the second stage, which has a mechanical advantage of 4. If an effort of 25,N is applied to the first stage, what load can the second stage raise?
questions.explanation:
The first stage produces an output force of


25×3=75,N


This becomes the effort on the second stage:


L=75×4=300,N


The correct answer is **C**, not D. The overall mechanical advantage is the product 3×4=12, giving 25×12=300,N.

questions.title: Lever with bar weight and an unknown fulcrum position
questions.question: A uniform 2.4,m bar weighs 120,N. A 300,N load acts at the left end, and a downward effort of 100,N acts at the right end. The bar balances horizontally. Find the distance of the fulcrum from the left end.
questions.explanation:
Let the fulcrum be x metres from the left end. The bar's weight acts at its centre, 1.2,m from the left end.

For equilibrium, the upward and downward moments about the fulcrum must balance. The downward effort at the right end and the bar's weight contribute clockwise moments if the fulcrum lies left of the centre.

Using moments about the left end is not sufficient because the reaction at the fulcrum is unknown. Taking moments about the fulcrum:


300x=100(2.4-x)+120(1.2-x)



300x=240-100x+144-120x



520x=384



x≈0.738,m


The nearest listed answer is 0.8,m, but the exact value does not match. This question should be recalibrated rather than treated as an exact multiple-choice item.

questions.question: A 400,N load is pulled up a rough inclined plane of length 5,m and height 3,m. The effort parallel to the plane is 300,N. Calculate the work done against friction.

W_f=1500-1200=300,J

questions.question: A uniform 1.5,m bar weighs 60,N. The fulcrum is at the centre. A load of 200,N acts 0.5,m to the left of the fulcrum, and an upward effort acts 0.75,m to the right. Find the effort required for equilibrium.

200(0.5)=E(0.75)



E=(100 / 0.75)=133.3,N

questions.title: Movable pulley: Acceleration is not constant speed
questions.question: A 180,N load is attached to an ideal movable pulley. The upward effort is 120,N. What is the net force on the movable assembly, including the load, and in which direction does it act? Ignore the pulley’s mass.

options.text: 60,N upward
60,N downward
120,N upward
Zero

questions.explanation:
Two rope segments each have tension 120,N, so the total upward force is


2T=240,N


The downward load is 180,N, giving a net force of


240-180=60,N


The net force is actually **60,N upward**, so the correct answer is **A**, not B. A downward net force would occur only if the total downward force exceeded the upward support.

Since W_{out}=Lh,


L=(2400 / 4)=600,N

questions.question: A weightless lever has a load of 240,N acting 25,cm from the fulcrum. An effort is applied 50,cm from the fulcrum at 30^° to the vertical. Find the effort required for equilibrium.

questions.title: Reversibility through a glass slab
questions.question: A ray passes from air through a parallel-sided glass slab and emerges into air with a lateral displacement of d. The entire ray path is then reversed, with light entering from the original emergent side along the exact reverse direction. Which statement is correct?
questions.diagramSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 460 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc; border-radius:8px; border:1px solid #cbd5e1; font-family:system-ui, sans-serif;">
      <text x="230" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#0f172a">Refraction Through Glass Slab: Lateral Displacement</text>
      <!-- Glass slab -->
      <rect x="100" y="65" width="260" height="70" fill="#e0f2fe" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="1.8"/>
      <text x="330" y="105" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#0369a1">Glass (Dense)</text>
      <!-- Incident Ray -->
      <line x1="60" y1="25" x2="160" y2="65" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
      <!-- Refracted Ray inside slab (bends towards normal) -->
      <line x1="160" y1="65" x2="220" y2="135" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
      <!-- Emergent Ray (parallel to incident) -->
      <line x1="220" y1="135" x2="320" y2="175" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
      <!-- Dotted original path -->
      <line x1="160" y1="65" x2="380" y2="153" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>
      <!-- Lateral displacement line -->
      <line x1="270" y1="155" x2="285" y2="115" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <text x="310" y="140" font-size="9" font-weight="700" fill="#16a34a">Lateral Displacement (d)</text>
      <text x="230" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#334155">Angle of Incidence i = Angle of Emergence e; Emergent ray is parallel to incident ray</text>
    </svg>

options.text: The lateral displacement becomes zero because the ray is reversed.
The ray retraces the original path in reverse, preserving the magnitude of the lateral displacement.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection at the first surface regardless of incidence angle.
The reversed ray emerges perpendicular to the original incident ray.

questions.explanation: The laws of refraction are reversible. A ray travelling backwards along an existing path retraces it exactly in reverse. Its lateral displacement has the same magnitude; reversing the direction does not eliminate the displacement.

questions.question: Light travels from air into glass. A ray is incident at 60^° and refracts at 35^°. Calculate the refractive index of the glass relative to air.

Using Snell's law,


n=(sin i / sin r)
=(sin60^° / sin35^°)



n=(0.8660 / 0.5736)≈1.51

questions.question: Light passes from air into medium A and then into medium B through parallel interfaces. The absolute refractive indices are 1.6 for A and 1.2 for B. The angle of incidence in air is 45^°. Which conclusion is correct if the ray propagates through both interfaces?

options.text: The ray undergoes total internal reflection at the A–B interface because 1.6>1.2.
The ray emerges into B at 45^°, since the first and second interfaces are parallel.
The ray travels at approximately 36.1^° to the normal in B.
The ray travels at approximately 53.1^° to the normal in B.

questions.explanation:
At parallel interfaces, Snell's law gives


1sin45^°=1.2sin r_B



sin r_B=(0.7071 / 1.2)=0.5893


Therefore,


r_B≈36.1^°


The ray can propagate through B because the angle in A is below the critical angle for the A–B interface. The final angle depends on the refractive index of B relative to air, not merely on the fact that the interfaces are parallel.

questions.question: Consider the following statements: I. Frequency remains unchanged when light crosses a stationary boundary. II. A parallel-sided slab produces lateral displacement for oblique incidence, even though the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray. III. Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a denser to a rarer medium and the incidence angle is smaller than the critical angle. IV. I, II and IV only.
II, III and IV only.
I, II, III and IV.

questions.explanation:
- I is true: frequency remains unchanged at a stationary boundary.
- II is true: parallel slab faces restore the emergent direction but generally leave lateral displacement.
- III is false: total internal reflection requires an incidence angle greater than the critical angle.
- IV is true because C=sin^{-1}(1/n) for a medium surrounded by air.

Therefore, I, II and IV are correct.

questions.question: Assertion (A):** The frequency of monochromatic light remains unchanged when it passes from air into glass. **Reason (R):** The frequency is determined by the source, and the wave oscillations must remain continuous across the stationary boundary.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.explanation:
Frequency during refraction

**Assertion (A):** The frequency of monochromatic light remains unchanged when it passes from air into glass.

**Reason (R):** The frequency is determined by the source, and the wave oscillations must remain continuous across the stationary boundary.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** The frequency remains constant across a stationary interface. The speed and wavelength change to satisfy v=flambda. Both statements are true, and the reason explains the assertion.

Medium Q must have a higher refractive index because the ray changes direction.

questions.explanation: Bending away from the normal indicates that the ray enters a medium with a lower refractive index, for the given light and under the stated assumptions. The frequency does not change at the boundary. A change in direction does not imply a zero refractive index.

Two small objects lie at different real depths in the same water, viewed nearly normally from air. Object A is 8 cm below the surface and object B is 12 cm below it. If the refractive index of water is 4/3, what are their apparent depths?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="48" width="300" height="142" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.18" /><path d="M10 48 H310" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><circle cx="95" cy="150" r="5" fill="#D97706" /><circle cx="230" cy="150" r="5" fill="#0D9488" /><circle cx="95" cy="124" r="4" fill="#D97706" fill-opacity="0.6" /><circle cx="230" cy="114" r="4" fill="#0D9488" fill-opacity="0.6" /><path d="M95 150 L140 48 L183 18 M230 150 L265 48 L291 18" stroke="#64748B" stroke-dasharray="4 3" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><text x="15" y="30" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air</text><text x="15" y="68" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Water</text><text x="105" y="128" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Image A</text><text x="238" y="111" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Image B</text><text x="65" y="174" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Object A</text><text x="200" y="174" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Object B</text></svg>

options.text: A: 8 cm; B: 12 cm
A: 6 cm; B: 9 cm
A: 2 cm; B: 3 cm

questions.explanation:
For near-normal viewing,


d_{apparent}=frac{d_{real}}{n}


For A,


d_A=(8 / 4/3)=6 cm


For B,


d_B=(12 / 4/3)=9 cm


Both objects appear raised towards the surface. Option A reverses the real-to-apparent depth ratio.

questions.question: The ray crosses media with known absolute refractive indices; the question concerns B relative to A. The absolute refractive indices of media A and B are 1.50 and 1.25, respectively. What is the refractive index of B relative to A?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="12" y="10" width="296" height="48" fill="#94A3B8" fill-opacity="0.15" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><rect x="12" y="60" width="296" height="48" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.22" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><rect x="12" y="110" width="296" height="58" fill="#0D9488" fill-opacity="0.12" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><text x="24" y="29" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air: n = 1</text><text x="24" y="79" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Medium A: n = 1.5</text><text x="24" y="132" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Medium B: n = 1.25</text><path d="M80 16 L110 60 L123 108 L139 160" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M139 160 L134 151 M139 160 L145 152" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /></svg>
questions.explanation:
The relative refractive index of B with respect to A is


n_{BA}=(n_B / n_A)
=(1.25 / 1.50)
=frac56≈0.833


Option A gives the reciprocal, n_{AB}, rather than B relative to A.

questions.title: Comparing incidence angle with the critical angle
questions.question: A ray is incident from glass of refractive index 1.5 into air at 40^°. The critical angle for the glass–air interface is approximately 41.8^°. The incident ray makes an angle of 40^° with the normal. Which statement is correct?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="8" y="90" width="304" height="78" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" /><path d="M8 90 H312 M160 15 V168" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><path d="M55 145 L160 90 L244 32" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M160 90 L244 32" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="18" y="110" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Glass</text><text x="18" y="20" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air</text><text x="168" y="26" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Normal</text><text x="75" y="130" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">i = 40°</text><text x="220" y="24" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Refracted ray</text></svg>

options.text: Total internal reflection occurs because 40^° is close to the critical angle.
The ray is reflected completely because the incident medium is glass.
The refracted angle is 41.8^°.
The ray refracts into air at an angle greater than 40^°, but less than 90^°.

questions.explanation:
Since 40^°<41.8^°, total internal reflection does not occur. By Snell's law,


1.5sin40^°=sin r



sin r≈0.9642


Therefore, r≈74.6^°, which is greater than 40^° but less than 90^°. Option A incorrectly assumes that being close to the critical angle is sufficient for total internal reflection.

questions.question: The incident ray is inside the denser medium; the refracted ray travels along the interface. A ray strikes a glass–air interface at its critical angle. Which statement correctly distinguishes this situation from total internal reflection?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="90" width="300" height="75" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" /><path d="M10 90 H310 M160 15 V165" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><path d="M65 145 L160 90 L278 90" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M266 83 L278 90 L266 97" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><text x="18" y="111" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Denser medium</text><text x="18" y="22" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Rarer medium</text><text x="174" y="79" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">r = 90°</text><text x="81" y="130" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">i = C</text></svg>

options.text: At the critical angle, the refracted ray travels along the interface; total internal reflection occurs when the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle.
At the critical angle, the incident ray travels along the interface, while the refracted ray returns into glass.
At the critical angle, the refracted ray bends towards the normal and enters air.
At the critical angle, both the incident and refracted rays make angles of 90^° with the normal.

questions.explanation: At the critical angle, the angle of refraction is 90^°. The incident angle itself is less than 90^°. Total internal reflection begins when the incidence angle is greater than the critical angle. Option D confuses the incident angle with the refracted angle.

questions.title: Choosing the correct prism arrangement for deviation
questions.question: Arrangement I Arrangement II Both arrangements use a right-angled isosceles prism. The intended internal incidence at the hypotenuse is 45^°. A glass prism has refractive index 1.5. A ray enters normally through one short face and strikes the hypotenuse at 45^°. Which statement about using the prism as a reflector is correct?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 140 120" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M20 100 L20 20 L120 100 Z" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.22" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" /><path d="M2 65 L20 65 L20 100" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.2" fill="none" /><path d="M20 65 L58 65 L58 25" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.2" fill="none" /><text x="24" y="112" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Right angle</text></svg>

options.text: The prism cannot reflect the ray internally because a glass surface always refracts light into air.
The prism can act as a reflector because 45^° exceeds the glass–air critical angle, so total internal reflection occurs at the hypotenuse.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection only when the hypotenuse is parallel to the incident ray.
The ray emerges undeviated through the hypotenuse because the incident ray entered normally through another face.

questions.explanation:
For glass of refractive index 1.5,


C=sin^{-1}≤ft((1 / 1.5)right)
≈41.8^°


Since 45^°>C, total internal reflection occurs at the hypotenuse. A right-angled isosceles prism can therefore change the direction of a ray by 90^° in this arrangement.

questions.title: Refraction through a prism versus a rectangular slab
questions.question: Parallel slab Triangular prism The slab has parallel faces; the prism has non-parallel refracting faces. A ray passes obliquely through a rectangular glass slab and then through a triangular glass prism of the same material. Which difference is expected when both are surrounded by air and total internal reflection is absent?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 140 115" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="30" y="15" width="80" height="85" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" /><path d="M3 85 L30 64 L110 42 L137 21" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.2" fill="none" /><path d="M3 85 L30 64 L110 42 L137 21" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.2" fill="none" /></svg>

options.text: Both emergent rays must be parallel to their respective incident rays.
The slab produces angular deviation but no lateral displacement, whereas the prism produces neither.
The slab's emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, whereas the prism generally produces an angular deviation because its refracting faces are not parallel.
The prism produces no refraction because the two faces have different orientations.

questions.explanation: A parallel-sided slab produces equal and opposite angular changes at its two surfaces, leaving the emergent ray parallel to the incident ray but laterally displaced. A triangular prism has non-parallel refracting faces, so the deviations generally do not cancel. Option A incorrectly applies the slab result to a prism.

Move the apparent image deeper because refraction always increases apparent depth.
Place the apparent image exactly on the water surface, irrespective of the object's depth.
Remove the backward extension because a virtual image cannot be formed by refraction.

questions.explanation: When light travels from water to air, it bends away from the normal. The eye traces the refracted rays backwards in straight lines, locating a virtual image closer to the surface than the real object. Option B reverses the direction of the apparent shift.

questions.question: The proposed fibre has a core of lower refractive index than its surrounding cladding. A student proposes an optical fibre with core refractive index 1.40 and cladding refractive index 1.50. The diagram shows light zigzagging inside the core by total internal reflection. What is the fundamental problem?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 165" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="12" y="35" width="296" height="100" rx="4" fill="#94A3B8" fill-opacity="0.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" /><rect x="12" y="57" width="296" height="56" rx="2" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.25" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="1.2" /><path d="M18 85 L68 60 L118 108 L168 60 L218 108 L280 85" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><text x="18" y="26" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Cladding: n = 1.50</text><text x="18" y="76" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Core: n = 1.40</text><text x="18" y="153" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Proposed fibre arrangement</text></svg>

options.text: The refractive index of the core must be exactly 1.
Total internal reflection is impossible at every interface between transparent materials.
The refractive index of the cladding must be lower than that of the core for the intended guiding mechanism; the proposed arrangement cannot support that mechanism at the core–cladding boundary.
The speed of light must be higher in the cladding than in a vacuum.

questions.explanation: For conventional step-index optical fibre guiding, the core must have a higher refractive index than the cladding. The ray travelling in the core must encounter a boundary leading to a lower-index medium to undergo total internal reflection. Here, the cladding has the higher index, so the proposed ray path is not supported by the intended mechanism.

questions.question: Air close to a hot road is generally hotter and less optically dense than the air above it. A driver sees what appears to be a pool of water on a hot road, but no water is present. Which explanation best matches the ray diagram?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 155 H312" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.3" /><path d="M8 132 Q80 120 160 132 T312 132" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="4 3" fill="none" /><path d="M8 105 Q80 94 160 105 T312 105" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="4 3" fill="none" /><circle cx="48" cy="42" r="6" fill="#F59E0B" /><circle cx="48" cy="42" r="6" fill="#F59E0B" /><path d="M48 42 Q100 63 140 95 Q180 130 240 125" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M240 125 L230 119 M240 125 L232 132" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><path d="M240 125 L290 66" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="4 4" fill="none" /><text x="13" y="23" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Distant object</text><text x="13" y="171" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Hot road surface</text><text x="180" y="91" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Curved ray path</text><text x="220" y="153" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Apparent image</text></svg>

options.text: Water vapour forms a real reflecting pool on the road.

Light from the sky curves through atmospheric layers of varying refractive index; under suitable conditions, strong bending and total internal reflection near the hot surface can contribute to the apparent image.
The road emits blue light because its temperature is high.
The phenomenon occurs because the refractive index of air is zero near the road.

questions.explanation:
best matches the ray diagram?

A) Water vapour forms a real reflecting pool on the road.

B) Light from the sky curves through atmospheric layers of varying refractive index; under suitable conditions, strong bending and total internal reflection near the hot surface can contribute to the apparent image.

C) The road emits blue light because its temperature is high.

D) The phenomenon occurs because the refractive index of air is zero near the road.

**Correct Answer: B**

**Reason:**

A mirage is an atmospheric optical phenomenon caused by a temperature-dependent refractive-index gradient. Rays from the sky can curve through the layers, and under suitable conditions the ray path can involve total internal reflection. The eye traces the arriving rays backwards, producing an apparent image that resembles a water surface.

It doubles from approximately 2.67 cm to 5.33 cm.

The ray follows a different path because the prism's refractive index changes with direction.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection at every surface during reverse travel.
The ray emerges parallel to its original incident direction regardless of the prism angle.

questions.explanation: The laws of refraction and reflection are reversible. Reversing the direction along an established ray path makes the light retrace that path in reverse. It does not guarantee that the prism's emergent ray is parallel to the original incident ray.

questions.title: Combined critical angle and refractive-index reasoning
questions.question: A transparent material has refractive index 1.5. A ray travels inside it and strikes an air boundary at 40^°. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: Total internal reflection occurs because the refractive index is greater than 1.
The critical angle is approximately 41.8^°, so the ray refracts into air.
The critical angle is 48.2^°, so total internal reflection occurs.
The critical angle is 30^°, so the ray undergoes total internal reflection.

questions.explanation:
ing

A transparent material has refractive index 1.5. A ray travels inside it and strikes an air boundary at 40^°. Which conclusion is correct?

A) Total internal reflection occurs because the refractive index is greater than 1.

B) The critical angle is approximately 41.8^°, so the ray refracts into air.

C) The critical angle is 48.2^°, so total internal reflection occurs.

D) The critical angle is 30^°, so the ray undergoes total internal reflection.

**Correct Answer: B**

**Reason:**


C=sin^{-1}(1/1.5)≈41.8^°


Since 40^°<C, the ray refracts into air. The refracted angle is greater than 40^°, but less than 90^°. Option A incorrectly treats the denser-to-rarer condition as sufficient by itself.

questions.title: Assertion–Reason: Total internal reflection
questions.question: Assertion (A):** A ray travelling from glass into air at an incidence angle greater than the critical angle undergoes total internal reflection. **Reason (R):** At such an angle, Snell's law would require the sine of the refracted angle to exceed 1.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.explanation:
Total internal reflection

**Assertion (A):** A ray travelling from glass into air at an incidence angle greater than the critical angle undergoes total internal reflection.

**Reason (R):** At such an angle, Snell's law would require the sine of the refracted angle to exceed 1.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** For incidence beyond the critical angle, Snell's law cannot give a real refracted angle because it would require sin r>1. No ordinary refracted ray propagates into the rarer medium, so total internal reflection occurs.

questions.title: Assertion–Reason: Apparent depth
questions.question: Assertion (A):** A coin at the bottom of a water-filled vessel appears raised when viewed nearly normally from air. **Reason (R):** Light from the coin bends away from the normal when it travels from water into air.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.explanation:
Apparent depth

**Assertion (A):** A coin at the bottom of a water-filled vessel appears raised when viewed nearly normally from air.

**Reason (R):** Light from the coin bends away from the normal when it travels from water into air.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

B) Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.

C) A is true, but R is false.

D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** Light bends away from the normal as it enters air from water. The eye traces the refracted rays backwards, placing the apparent image above the real coin.

The boundary changes the propagation speed and wavelength, but the oscillation frequency remains fixed by the source and boundary continuity.
Frequency is proportional to the refractive index of every medium.
The ray stops oscillating momentarily at the boundary.

questions.explanation: The source determines the frequency. At a stationary boundary, frequency remains continuous while the speed and wavelength adjust to the new medium.

questions.title: Refraction through a layered medium
questions.question: Light travels from medium A into B and then into C through parallel interfaces. The refractive indices are 1.0, 1.5, and 1.2, respectively. Which statement is correct if the ray crosses both interfaces without total internal reflection?

options.text: The ray's frequency increases in B and decreases in C.
The ray bends towards the normal in B and then away from the normal in C; its final angle depends on the refractive index of C relative to A.
The ray must emerge parallel to its original direction because all interfaces are parallel, regardless of the final medium.
The ray's speed is the same in all three media.

questions.explanation: Entry from A into higher-index B causes bending towards the normal. Entry from B into lower-index C causes bending away from the normal. Since C has a different refractive index from A, the final direction need not match the original direction. Frequency remains unchanged throughout.

questions.question: A ray travels from air into a transparent medium of refractive index 1.4. If the angle of refraction is 30^°, calculate the angle of incidence.

sin i=1.4sin30^°=0.7


Therefore,


i=sin^{-1}(0.7)≈44.4^°

questions.title: Comparing light speeds in two media
questions.question: The speed of light in medium A is 2.5×10^8 m/s, while that in medium B is 2.0×10^8 m/s. What is the refractive index of B relative to A?
questions.explanation:
The relative refractive index of B with respect to A is


n_{BA}=(v_A / v_B)



n_{BA}=(2.5 / 2.0)=1.25


The relative refractive index is the inverse of the speed ratio. Option A gives v_B/v_A.

Given v=0.75c,


n=(c / v)=(c / 0.75c)
=frac1{0.75}=1.33


Option A gives v/c, the reciprocal of the refractive index.
