questions.title: Why an object seen through a plane glass window appears nearly in its true direction
questions.question: The window has parallel faces, and the ray emerges into air on the opposite side. An object is viewed through a thin, parallel-sided glass window. Why is the apparent direction of the emergent ray the same as the direction of the incident ray, even though the ray bends inside the glass?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 175" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="120" y="15" width="80" height="145" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.22" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" /><path d="M10 130 L120 105 L200 91 L306 66" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M10 130 L306 66" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="5 4" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><text x="126" y="32" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Glass window</text><text x="14" y="146" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Object</text><text x="238" y="56" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Observer</text></svg>

options.text: The refractive index of glass is identical to that of air.
The second surface cancels the first surface's refraction because both surfaces are parallel, although a lateral displacement may remain.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection twice, restoring its original direction.
The ray bends towards the normal at both surfaces by equal angles.

questions.explanation: The ray bends towards the normal on entering glass and away from the normal on leaving it. Parallel interfaces and the same external medium restore the original emergent direction. The emergent ray may still be laterally displaced. Option D is incorrect because the ray bends in opposite angular senses at the two interfaces.

questions.title: Correct use of a right-angled prism in a periscope
questions.question: A right-angled prism redirects a ray through 90^° using total internal reflection. A periscope uses a right-angled isosceles prism with refractive index 1.5. A ray enters normally through a short face and strikes the hypotenuse at 45^°. Which statement explains why this arrangement can replace a plane mirror?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M30 30 L30 105 L105 105 Z" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M30 30 L105 105 L180 30 Z" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M5 67 L30 67 L66 103 L66 145" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M66 145 L60 135 M66 145 L72 135" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><text x="14" y="20" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Incident light</text><text x="78" y="158" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Reflected ray</text><text x="128" y="52" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Prism</text></svg>

options.text: The ray undergoes total internal reflection at the hypotenuse and can be redirected through 90^° with very little loss at the reflecting surface.
The ray is refracted by 90^° because the prism's refractive index is 1.5.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection at the hypotenuse only if the refractive index is less than 1.
The ray is absorbed by the prism and re-emitted in a perpendicular direction.

questions.explanation: The critical angle for glass–air is approximately 41.8^°. The internal incidence angle of 45^° exceeds this value, so total internal reflection occurs. The ray is reflected through 90^° in this geometry, making the prism useful in optical instruments.

questions.question: The refracted ray makes a smaller angle with the normal than the incident ray. The ray diagram shows light entering medium Q from medium P and bending towards the normal. Which additional conclusion is valid, assuming the same frequency of light is maintained across the boundary?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 185" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 85 H310" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" /><rect x="10" y="87" width="300" height="82" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" /><path d="M45 20 L160 85 L270 146" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M160 12 V170" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="4 4" stroke-width="1.1" /><text x="17" y="18" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Medium P</text><text x="17" y="105" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Medium Q</text><text x="173" y="25" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Normal</text><text x="205" y="137" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Ray in Q</text></svg>

options.text: The speed of light increases in Q, and the wavelength increases.
The frequency increases in Q, while the speed remains constant.
The speed decreases in Q, and the wavelength decreases.
The speed decreases in Q, but the wavelength increases.

questions.explanation:
Bending towards the normal indicates entry into the optically denser medium for the given light. Thus the refractive index increases, and


v=(c / n)


decreases. Frequency remains unchanged, so lambda=v/f also decreases. Option D incorrectly predicts an increase in wavelength.

questions.title: Determining the refractive index from a ray diagram
questions.question: The angles shown are measured from the normal at the plane interface. The figure shows a ray passing from air into a transparent medium. The angle of incidence is 60^° and the angle of refraction is 35^°. Which is the approximate refractive index of the medium relative to air?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 195" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="98" width="300" height="85" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" /><path d="M10 98 H310" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M160 20 V182" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="4 4" stroke-width="1.1" /><path d="M48 26 L160 98 L196 180" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M48 26 L160 98" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="16" y="18" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air</text><text x="16" y="118" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Transparent medium</text><text x="105" y="49" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">i = 60°</text><text x="166" y="126" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">r = 35°</text><text x="170" y="30" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Normal</text></svg>
questions.explanation:
Using Snell's law,


n=(sin i / sin r)
=(sin60^° / sin35^°)



n=(0.8660 / 0.5736)≈1.51


The calculated value is approximately 1.51, so none of the listed options is correct as originally framed. To preserve accuracy, the question must be corrected.

**Corrected option D:** 1.51.

The other options are distractors arising from incorrect ratios or inaccurate trigonometric values.

options.text: The refractive index of glass is slightly higher for blue light than for red light, so blue light travels more slowly in the glass.
The refractive index of glass is higher for red light because red light has a longer wavelength.
Both colours must have the same refractive index because they travel through the same material.
Blue light has a higher frequency inside glass because it bends more strongly.

questions.explanation:
Greater bending towards the normal indicates a higher refractive index for blue light in this situation. Since


v=(c / n)


blue light travels more slowly in the glass. Its frequency remains unchanged at the boundary; the change in speed is accompanied by a change in wavelength.

dfrac{i}{r} is always equal to the absolute refractive index of medium 2.

questions.title: Previous Board Question, 2007 — Plane mirror versus total internal reflection
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes ordinary reflection at a plane mirror from total internal reflection at a suitable prism face?

options.text: A plane mirror always reflects all incident light, while total internal reflection absorbs it.
Total internal reflection requires light to travel from a rarer to a denser medium.
A plane mirror and total internal reflection always reflect exactly the same fraction of incident light.
Under ideal conditions, total internal reflection reflects the incident light back into the denser medium, whereas an ordinary mirror can have losses through absorption and transmission.

questions.explanation: Total internal reflection ideally reflects essentially all incident optical energy back into the denser medium. Real mirrors can absorb some light, and a glass mirror may transmit some light through its surfaces. The distinction is not that total internal reflection requires a rarer-to-denser transition.

questions.title: Previous Board Question, 2008 — Speed and wavelength in glass
questions.question: A monochromatic beam of wavelength lambda in air enters glass of refractive index 1.5. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The speed in glass is c/1.5, the wavelength becomes lambda/1.5, and the frequency remains unchanged.
The speed becomes 1.5c, and the wavelength remains unchanged.
The speed remains c, while the frequency decreases by a factor of 1.5.
Both the frequency and wavelength decrease by a factor of 1.5.

questions.explanation: The refractive index is n=c/v, so v=c/1.5. Since frequency is unchanged and v=flambda, the wavelength becomes lambda/1.5. The speed cannot increase to 1.5c.

questions.question: Which pair of conditions is necessary for total internal reflection?

options.text: Light travels from a rarer to a denser medium at any incidence angle.
Light strikes the interface normally while travelling from glass to air.
Light travels from an optically denser to an optically rarer medium, and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.
The angle of refraction must be smaller than the angle of incidence in every situation.

questions.explanation: Both conditions must be satisfied: the light must approach from the denser medium, and its incidence angle must be greater than the critical angle. At normal incidence, total internal reflection does not occur.

questions.title: Apparent depth in a two-layer liquid tank
questions.question: A tank contains two transparent liquid layers, each 6 cm thick. Their refractive indices are 1.2 and 1.5, respectively. A small object lies at the bottom. Viewed vertically from air, what is the apparent depth of the object below the top surface?

options.text: 12 cm
9 cm
8 cm
5 cm

questions.explanation:
For near-normal viewing through plane-parallel layers, the apparent depth is the sum of the apparent thicknesses:


d_{app}=(6 / 1.2)+(6 / 1.5)



d_{app}=5+4=9 cm


**Correction:** The correct answer is **B, 9 cm**. Option C incorrectly combines the layers using an inappropriate single refractive index.

questions.title: Comparing apparent shifts in two media
questions.question: Two liquids have refractive indices 1.25 and 1.6. Objects are placed at the same real depth of 16 cm in both liquids and viewed normally from air. What is the difference in their apparent shifts?

options.text: 1.6 cm
2.8 cm
3.5 cm
4.0 cm

questions.explanation:
For the first liquid,


d₁=(16 / 1.25)=12.8 cm


Shift =16-12.8=3.2 cm.

For the second liquid,


d₂=(16 / 1.6)=10 cm


Shift =16-10=6 cm.

Difference:


6-3.2=2.8 cm

questions.title: Comparing speeds using critical angles
questions.question: Two transparent media P and Q have critical angles 30^° and 45^°, respectively, when surrounded by air. What is the ratio of the speed of light in P to that in Q?

options.text: 1:sqrt2
1:sqrt3
sqrt2:1

questions.explanation:
The absolute refractive index is n=1/sin C, and speed is inversely proportional to refractive index. Thus,


(v_P / v_Q)=(n_Q / n_P)
=(1/sin45^° / 1/sin30^°)



(v_P / v_Q)=(0.5 / 0.7071)
=frac1{sqrt2}


**Correction:** The ratio is 1:sqrt2, so **A is the correct answer**.

questions.question: A submerged object has an apparent upward shift of 5 cm. The liquid's refractive index is 1.25. Calculate the real depth.

25 cm
15 cm

questions.explanation:
Let the real depth be d. Then


d_{app}=(d / 1.25)


The apparent shift is


d-(d / 1.25)=5



d-0.8d=5



0.2d=5Rightarrow d=25 cm

questions.question: Light travels from air into medium A with refractive index 1.5, and then into medium B with refractive index 1.2. The two interfaces are parallel. If the angle of incidence in air is 60^°, calculate the angle the ray makes with the normal inside medium B.

questions.title: Finding the wavelength in a transparent medium
questions.question: Light of frequency 6×10^ Hz travels through glass of refractive index 1.5. What is its wavelength in glass?

options.text: 500 nm
333 nm
750 nm
250 nm

questions.explanation:
The speed in glass is


v=(3×10^8 / 1.5)=2×10^8 m/s


Therefore,


lambda=(v / f)
=(2×10^8 / 6×10^{14)}
=3.33×10^{-7} m


Thus,


lambda≈333 nm


Option A corresponds approximately to the wavelength in vacuum, not in glass.

questions.question: The experiment shows a ray reflecting inside glass at the glass–air boundary. A student wants to demonstrate total internal reflection using a glass block and air. Which experimental change would definitely prevent total internal reflection at the interface, regardless of the incidence angle used in the original setup?
questions.diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="92" width="300" height="82" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" /><path d="M10 92 H310" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M160 15 V174" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="4 4" stroke-width="1.2" /><path d="M45 145 L160 92 L270 145" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M261 139 L270 145 L260 150" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><text x="18" y="20" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air</text><text x="18" y="112" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Glass</text><text x="170" y="27" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Normal</text><text x="74" y="132" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Incident ray</text><text x="216" y="132" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Reflected ray</text></svg>

options.text: Increase the incidence angle while keeping the light in glass and the other medium as air.
Replace air with a medium whose refractive index is lower than that of glass.
Use a glass block with a higher refractive index while maintaining incidence above the new critical angle.
Reverse the direction of light so that it travels from air into glass.

questions.explanation: Total internal reflection requires light to travel from an optically denser to an optically rarer medium. Reversing the direction so that light travels from air into glass removes this necessary condition. Options A and C can preserve total internal reflection, while B still permits it because the surrounding medium remains optically rarer than glass.

questions.title: Previous Board Question, 2014 — Glass slab versus triangular prism
questions.question: A ray passes through a rectangular glass slab and then through a triangular glass prism, each surrounded by air. Which statement correctly compares their emergent directions?

options.text: Both emergent rays are necessarily parallel to their respective incident rays.
The slab causes angular deviation, but the prism produces only lateral displacement.
Neither produces any change in the ray's direction.
The slab's emergent ray is parallel to its incident ray, whereas the prism generally produces angular deviation because its refracting faces are not parallel.

questions.explanation: Parallel slab faces cancel the angular deviation, although lateral displacement remains. A prism has inclined faces, so the angular changes generally do not cancel. The emergent ray is therefore generally not parallel to the incident ray.

questions.explanation:
ing

Two convex lenses are made from the same glass. Lens A has more strongly curved surfaces than lens B. Assuming comparable surface shapes and the same surrounding medium, which statement is generally correct?

A) Lens A has greater power and a shorter focal-length magnitude.

B) Lens A has smaller power and a longer focal-length magnitude.

C) Both must have equal focal lengths because they are made from the same glass.

D) The focal lengths depend only on the masses of the lenses.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** For the same refractive index and surrounding medium, stronger surface curvature generally gives greater optical power. Since P=1/f, greater power corresponds to a shorter focal-length magnitude.

options.text: The lens changes its physical shape on immersion.
The liquid absorbs the converging rays.
Every convex lens has negative power in a liquid.
The lens has a lower refractive index than the surrounding liquid, reversing its usual optical behaviour.

questions.explanation: Lens power depends on the refractive index of the lens relative to the surrounding medium. If the lens has a lower refractive index than the liquid, a convex lens can behave as a diverging lens. Option C incorrectly claims that every convex lens has negative power in a liquid.

The image is inverted, so its signed height is negative:

questions.title: Object and image on the same side
questions.question: A lens forms a virtual image of a real object on the same side as the object. Which conclusion is necessarily correct?

options.text: The lens must be convex.
The image must be inverted.
The image distance is positive under the New Cartesian convention.
The image distance is negative under the New Cartesian convention.

questions.explanation: With light travelling from left to right, the object lies on the left and has negative object distance. A virtual image on the same side also has negative image distance. A concave lens always produces this type of image for a real object in air; a convex lens can do so when the object is inside its focal length.

questions.title: Lens power and magnification
questions.question: A convex lens has power +2.5 D. An object of height 4 cm is placed 60 cm in front of it. What is the image height?

options.text: +8 cm
-8 cm
+2 cm
-2 cm

questions.explanation:
f=frac1{2.5}=0.4 m=40 cm


With u=-60 cm,


frac1v-frac1{-60}=frac1{40}



frac1v=frac1{40}-frac1{60}=frac1{120}


Therefore, v=+120 cm, and


m=frac vu=(120 / -60)=-2.


Hence h_i=mh_o=-2(4)=-8 cm.

**Correct Answer: B**, not D. The image is inverted and twice the object's height.
questions.question_skeleton: a convex lens has power # d an object of height # cm is placed # cm in front of it what is the image height

questions.title: Correcting a misconception
questions.question: A student says, “A convex lens always forms a real image because it is a converging lens.” Which response is best?

options.text: Correct, because a converging lens cannot form a virtual image.
Incorrect, because a convex lens forms a virtual, erect and magnified image when the object is inside its focal length.
Correct, except when the object is at 2F₁.
Incorrect, because a convex lens forms only virtual images.

questions.explanation: A convex lens normally forms real images when the object is beyond its principal focus. When the object is between the optical centre and focus, the refracted rays diverge and their backward extensions form a virtual, erect, magnified image.

questions.title: Equivalent lens power
questions.question: Three thin lenses in contact have powers +4 D, -1.5 D and -1.0 D. Which is the equivalent power and focal length?
questions.explanation:
P_{net}=4-1.5-1.0=+1.5 D



f=frac1{1.5} m=+0.667 m


So the focal length is approximately +66.7 cm.

questions.title: Image size and orientation
questions.question: An object of height 5 cm produces an image of height -15 cm. Which statement follows directly from the image-height information?

options.text: The image is virtual and diminished.
The image is real and three times the object's size, assuming the usual thin-lens setup for a real object.
The lens must be concave.
The focal length must be 15 cm.

questions.explanation:
The negative image height indicates inversion relative to the upright object, and the magnitude ratio is


|m|=≤ft|(-15 / 5)right|=3.


Thus, the image is inverted and three times the object's size. For a real object in the usual lens arrangement, this corresponds to a real image formed by a convex lens. The image height alone does not determine the focal length.

questions.title: A focal-length measurement setup
questions.question: In an ideal convex-lens experiment, an object is placed at the principal focus and a plane mirror is placed behind the lens. Which condition helps the rays return to the object point after reflection and a second passage through the lens?

options.text: The object must be at 2F₁.
The mirror must be placed at the optical centre.
The lens must be concave.
The object must be at the principal focus, so the outgoing rays are parallel before reflection.

questions.explanation: When the object is at the principal focus, rays emerging from the convex lens are parallel. A plane mirror reflects the parallel beam back, and the lens focuses the returning rays at the original focal point.

questions.title: Power and direction of convergence
questions.question: A lens has focal length +80 cm. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Its power is -1.25 D, and it is diverging.
Its power is +1.25 D, and it is converging.
Its power is +80 D, and it is converging.
Its power is -80 D, and it is diverging.

questions.explanation:
f=+0.80 m,quad P=frac1{0.80}=+1.25 D.


The positive focal length and power indicate a converging lens in air.

questions.title: Integrated image-formation problem
questions.question: A convex lens forms a real image at +40 cm when the object is at -20 cm. Which combination gives the focal length, magnification and image orientation?

options.text: f=+13.3 cm, m=-2, inverted
f=+20 cm, m=+2, erect
f=+13.3 cm, m=+2, erect
f=+60 cm, m=-0.5, inverted

questions.explanation:
frac1f=frac1v-frac1u
=frac1{40}-frac1{-20}



frac1f=frac1{40}+frac1{20}=frac3{40}



f=(40 / 3)≈+13.3 cm.


Magnification:


m=frac vu=(40 / -20)=-2.


The image is real, inverted and twice the object's size.

questions.title: Board-style Multiple statements about image formation
questions.question: Consider the following statements about a convex lens forming an image of a real object. I. An object beyond 2F₁ produces a real, inverted and diminished image between F₂ and 2F₂. II. An object at 2F₁ produces a real, inverted image of the same size at 2F₂. III. An object between F₁ and the optical centre produces a real, inverted and magnified image. Which statements are correct?

options.text: I only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.explanation: Statements I and II are standard convex-lens cases. Statement III is false: an object inside the focal length produces a **virtual, erect and magnified** image on the object's side.

questions.title: Board-style Two lenses in contact
questions.question: A convex lens of power +5 D is placed in contact with a concave lens of power -8 D. What is the equivalent focal length of the combination?
questions.explanation:
P_{net}=+5-8=-3 D



f=frac1{-3} m=-0.333 m


The equivalent focal length is approximately -33.3 cm, so the combination is diverging.

questions.title: Board-style Finding focal length from magnification
questions.question: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a convex lens. The image is real and inverted, with magnification -2. What is the focal length?

options.text: 10 cm
15 cm
20 cm
30 cm

questions.explanation:
m=frac vu=-2,quad u=-30 cm


Thus v=+60 cm. Using the lens formula,


frac1f=frac1v-frac1u
=frac1{60}+frac1{30}=frac1{20}.


Therefore, f=+20 cm.

questions.title: Board-style A virtual image from a convex lens
questions.question: A convex lens forms a virtual image three times the height of a real object. If the focal length is +24 cm, which object distance is correct?

options.text: -8 cm
-12 cm
-16 cm
-32 cm

questions.explanation:
For a virtual, erect image, m=+3, so


v=3u.


Using the lens formula,


frac1{3u}-frac1u=frac1{24}



-frac2{3u}=frac1{24}
Rightarrow u=-16 cm.


Therefore, **the correct answer is C, not A**. This correction illustrates why the sign convention must be applied consistently.

questions.title: Board-style Image position from focal length and object distance
questions.question: A convex lens has focal length 12 cm. An object is placed 18 cm in front of it. What is the image distance and nature?

options.text: +36 cm, real and inverted
-36 cm, virtual and erect
+7.2 cm, real and diminished
-7.2 cm, virtual and erect

questions.explanation:
u=-18 cm,quad f=+12 cm



frac1v-frac1{-18}=frac1{12}
Rightarrow frac1v=frac1{12}-frac1{18}=frac1{36}.


Thus v=+36 cm. A positive image distance means a real image on the opposite side.
